subtype: Following with the eyes and joint attention [Expressing]
passage:
“Kishore, where's Papa?” asked Ujjwal, walking across the room. Kishore's eyes followed him step by step.
“Look, Kishore. Kite!” Ujjwal pointed out of the window at a red kite over the rooftops.
Kishore turned his head to the window, then back at his father's face. “Kite,” he said, pointing too.
“Yes, kite! You saw it.”
Kishore kept watching until the red shape slid behind the water tank.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal point at through the window?
qa.a: A red kite over the rooftops.

qa.q: What does Kishore's glance back at his father seem to show?
qa.a: It seems to show he was interested and wanted to share the sight with Ujjwal. It could also be that he was checking whether the word Ujjwal used was the right one.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do next to keep the shared looking going?
qa.a: He could point at other things, say their names, and pause to see whether Kishore looks where he points.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel when Kishore follows his point?
qa.a: He is likely to feel delighted and connected, because his son is looking with him and not just at him. 🙂

grounding: A toddler tracks a parent with his eyes and follows a point to share attention on an object.

subtype: Following with the eyes and joint attention [Expressing]
passage: Playgroup note, Friday. Ayesha, almost two, watched me across the room while I set out cups, turning her head as I moved. When I pointed to the picture of a cat on the wall and said “Look, a cat,” she looked at the cat, then at me, and pointed too. She stayed with the picture for a long moment. I said “cat” again and waved at it. I will tell her mother how well she looks along with us. 🙂 Kavitha

qa.q: Who wrote the note, and what did Ayesha look at after the pointing?
qa.a: Kavitha wrote it, and Ayesha looked at the picture of a cat on the wall.

qa.q: What does Ayesha's look from the cat to Kavitha suggest she was thinking?
qa.a: It suggests she was interested and wanted to share the cat with Kavitha, since she pointed as well. It could also mean she was checking Kavitha's reaction.

qa.q: What might Kavitha say to Ayesha's mother?
qa.a: Kavitha might describe what they saw, that Ayesha follows a pointing finger and shares her attention, and if the mother has any questions about her child's development she can ask a paediatrician.

qa.q: How might Ayesha see Kavitha's naming of the cat?
qa.a: She may feel that her attention is noticed and welcomed, and that a shared look comes with a word attached, which helps her learn.

grounding: A toddler follows a caregiver with her eyes and looks where the adult points, sharing attention on an object.

subtype: Looking away when overwhelmed [Regulating]
passage: Observation note, Sunday. At Aadhya's second birthday, the room filled with clapping, music and an uncle leaning in close to say “Boo!” Aadhya's eyes slid away from him to the floor, and she held the edge of my sari. She stayed like that, looking at the pattern on the rug, breathing slowly. I asked the uncle to sit back and talk softly. After a few minutes she looked up again and gave him a small smile. 🙂 Yash

qa.q: What was Aadhya looking at when she turned her eyes away?
qa.a: She looked at the floor and the pattern on the rug.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya look away from the uncle, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: She was probably overwhelmed by the noise and the close face, and looking away helped her settle. It might also have been simple tiredness, but her smile once things calmed suggests it was not rejection.

qa.q: What did Yash do that helped Aadhya?
qa.a: Yash asked the uncle to sit back and speak softly, so the room felt less intense and Aadhya could return on her own.

qa.q: How might the uncle feel when Aadhya looks away?
qa.a: He might feel a little rebuffed at first, but knowing it is a break for her, he can wait and greet her gently later.

grounding: A toddler turns her eyes away from a loud and intense interaction to calm down, and the adult lowers the intensity.

subtype: Looking away when overwhelmed [Regulating]
passage: The wedding drums pounded in the village square. Sarita, two, sat on her uncle Vijay's knee at the edge of the crowd. He put his face close to hers, grinning, and shouted “Hello, my princess!” Her eyes swung away to the bangle on her wrist and stayed there. Her thumb went into her mouth. Vijay stopped shouting, sat back, and said quietly, “Big noise, isn't it?” After a minute, Sarita glanced up at him and held out the bangle for him to see.

qa.q: Where was Sarita sitting?
qa.a: On her uncle Vijay's knee at the edge of the crowd in the village square.

qa.q: What did Sarita feel when she looked at her bangle, and what might it also mean?
qa.a: She probably felt overwhelmed by the noise and his loud face, so she looked at something quiet. It could also be shyness, but holding out the bangle later shows she was not rejecting him.

qa.q: What could Vijay try to help Sarita enjoy the wedding?
qa.a: He could sit a little further from the drums, keep his voice soft and let her come back to him when she is ready.

qa.q: What might the evening be like for Sarita from her seat?
qa.a: Everything is loud, bright and fast, and she cannot walk away, so looking at a small quiet object may be the only break she can give herself.

grounding: A toddler turns her eyes away from an overwhelming loud interaction to calm down, and the adult lowers the intensity.

subtype: Puffed cheeks and cheek raising in play [Expressing]
passage: In a kitchen in Lisbon, Clara puffed out her cheeks like a fish and let the air go with a pop. Her toddler Kaito stared. Then he filled his own cheeks, eyes wide with effort, and squeezed them with both palms until the air burst out. He laughed so hard that his cheeks rose high and round. Clara did it again, and Kaito copied her, this time getting it just right. “Fish face,” she said, and he lifted his chin, pleased.

qa.q: Where did Clara puff out her cheeks?
qa.a: In a kitchen in Lisbon.

qa.q: What is Kaito feeling as he puffs his cheeks and laughs?
qa.a: He is probably having fun and feeling proud of copying his mother, as the laughter and lifted chin suggest. It could also be that he simply likes the popping sensation.

qa.q: What could Clara do to build on the game?
qa.a: She could try other faces such as a big smile or a wide mouth and let Kaito copy each one. 😊

qa.q: What might Clara notice about Kaito's growth from this game?
qa.a: She might see that he controls his face better than before and that he wants to join her in play.

grounding: A toddler puffs his cheeks in an imitation game and raises them in a big laugh, showing fun and copying skills.

subtype: Puffed cheeks and cheek raising in play [Expressing]
passage: At the bus stop I watched a toddler called Zubin sitting in a pushchair opposite his big sister Afreen. She puffed her cheeks and made a popping sound. Zubin puffed his too, red-faced, eyes fixed on her mouth. When she broke into a grin, his cheeks rose up round his eyes in a big smile. I can't know what he was thinking, but he looked delighted to be copying her. The bus arrived and Afreen blew him a fish-pop kiss.

qa.q: Who was Zubin copying at the bus stop?
qa.a: His big sister Afreen.

qa.q: What does the observer think Zubin felt, and how sure is the observer?
qa.a: The narrator thinks he was delighted to copy his sister, judging by his fixed look and big smile, but says they cannot know what he was thinking.

qa.q: What could Afreen try next with Zubin?
qa.a: She could invent a new face for him to copy, and watch his eyes to see if he still wants to play.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel about being copied?
qa.a: She may feel proud and grown-up that her little brother wants to do what she does, and enjoy having a play partner. 😊

grounding: A toddler puffs his cheeks in imitation and raises them in a big smile, as an observer sees.

subtype: Wrinkled nose at smells and tastes [Expressing]
passage: At the family's tea stall in the village, Shreya's mother Nazia lifted a spoon of methi sabzi to the toddler's lips. Shreya's nose wrinkled up and she pressed her lips shut, head pulled back. “Not yet, then,” said Nazia, and set the spoon down without fuss. Shreya ate her roti and dal instead. Two days later Nazia put a tiny bit of the sabzi beside the dal. Shreya sniffed it, wrinkled her nose again, but licked a corner and looked at her mother.

qa.q: What did Nazia offer Shreya at the tea stall?
qa.a: A spoonful of methi sabzi.

qa.q: What does Shreya's wrinkled nose suggest she felt, and what else might it mean?
qa.a: It suggests dislike of the smell or strange taste, since she pulled her head back too. It might also mean she was simply not hungry for something new.

qa.q: How did Nazia handle the refusal, and what could she try next?
qa.a: She did not force it and offered it again later in a tiny amount. Next she could let Shreya see her eating it happily.

qa.q: What might Shreya feel when her mother lets it go?
qa.a: She may feel that her signal was heard, which lets her feel safe enough to try a lick another day. 🙂

grounding: A toddler wrinkles her nose at an unfamiliar food, and the adult respects the reaction and tries again later.

subtype: Wrinkled nose at smells and tastes [Expressing]
passage: Chen opened the fridge and Javier, two, standing at his knee in a Vancouver kitchen, suddenly wrinkled his whole nose and turned his face away. “Blue cheese,” said Chen, and laughed. “Strong smell, huh?” Javier waved a hand in front of his face. Chen closed the fridge door, took a slice of plain cheese instead and cut it into little pieces. Javier ate one, then another. The blue cheese stayed at the back of the shelf.

qa.q: What did Javier react to when Chen opened the fridge?
qa.a: The strong smell of the blue cheese.

qa.q: What did Javier's wrinkled nose and waving hand show he felt?
qa.a: They show dislike of the strong smell. It could also mean he was startled by the sudden odour, not that he disliked cheese in general.

qa.q: What did Chen do that respected Javier's reaction?
qa.a: He shut the fridge and offered a milder cheese instead of asking Javier to try the smelly one.

qa.q: How might Javier see Chen's laughter?
qa.a: He may see it as friendly, a sign that the smell is a normal thing to notice and that his reaction was understood. 🙂

grounding: A toddler wrinkles his nose at a bad smell, and the adult respects it without forcing food.

subtype: Puckering and lip stretching [Expressing]
passage:
“Jasleen, give Nani a kiss goodnight,” said Rajni. Jasleen leaned over, lips pushed into a small round pucker, and pressed them against the phone screen.
“Mmmwah!” said Nani from the phone.
“Now shoes,” said Rajni. Jasleen sat down and sucked her lips in, tongue out a little, pulling at a strap.
“You're working hard.”
Then the doorbell rang and Jasleen stretched her lips wide and squealed, “Papa!”

qa.q: What did Jasleen press her puckered lips against?
qa.a: The phone screen, to kiss Nani goodnight.

qa.q: What might Jasleen's stretched lips and squeal at the doorbell mean, and what alternative is there?
qa.a: They most likely show excitement that Papa is home. They might also just be a loud reaction to the doorbell sound.

qa.q: What could Rajni do to build on this play?
qa.a: Rajni could name each feeling as it happens, like “You're excited!”, and copy the kiss or the squeal back playfully.

qa.q: How might Nani feel receiving a kiss through the phone?
qa.a: She probably feels loved and delighted that her granddaughter did it on her own, even from far away.

grounding: A toddler puckers for a kiss, sucks in her lips in concentration and stretches them in an excited squeal.

subtype: Puckering and lip stretching [Expressing]
passage: Playgroup note, Wednesday. Pallavi, two, puckered her lips and gave her doll a loud kiss during the tea-party game. Later, threading big wooden beads, she pulled her lips tightly in and held them there until the bead went on. When rain began on the roof, she stretched her mouth wide and squealed with her arms flapping. Same little mouth, three different meanings. I will keep watching what she is doing each time before guessing. 🙂 Himani

qa.q: What was Pallavi doing when she sucked her lips in?
qa.a: She was threading big wooden beads.

qa.q: What did Pallavi's wide mouth and squeal at the rain show she was feeling?
qa.a: It probably shows excitement, since her arms flapped as well. It could also be a reaction to the sudden sound of rain on the roof.

qa.q: What is Himani's plan for reading Pallavi's mouth shapes?
qa.a: Himani will look at what Pallavi is doing each time before guessing, because the same lip movement can mean different things.

qa.q: How might Pallavi's mother feel hearing this?
qa.a: She may enjoy hearing her daughter is exploring so many ways to show feelings, and may notice them herself at home.

grounding: A toddler puckers, tightens and stretches her lips in different contexts, each with a different meaning.

subtype: Trembling lip before crying [Expressing]
passage: The cousins had left after the holiday and the flat felt very quiet. Farhan, two, stood by the front door, looking at the empty shoe rack. His lower lip began to tremble and turned down at the corners, and his eyes shone. Ganga lifted him onto her hip. “You miss them,” she said softly, rocking a little. Farhan pressed his face to her neck and let out a shaky breath, and then the tears came slowly.

qa.q: What was Farhan looking at when his lip began to tremble?
qa.a: The empty shoe rack by the front door.

qa.q: What might Farhan feel when his lip trembles, and what else could it be?
qa.a: He probably feels sad that his cousins have gone, as he stared at the empty rack. It could also be that the quiet flat felt strange to him.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that helped?
qa.a: She picked him up, spoke softly and named the feeling, which gave him closeness while he cried.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel seeing him this way?
qa.a: She may feel tender toward him and a little sad herself, and she might be glad he can show her his feelings.

grounding: A toddler's lower lip trembles before crying from sadness, and a soothing voice and closeness help.

subtype: Trembling lip before crying [Expressing]
passage:
“Harsha, what happened to your biscuit?” asked Uday.
Harsha looked at the crumbs on the floor. Her lower lip curled down and started to wobble.
“Oh, it broke. Come here.” He sat and opened his arms.
“Bis-cuit,” she said thickly.
“I know, it broke and you're sad.” He hugged her and rubbed her back. “We'll get another one.”
Harsha's lip stopped trembling and she sniffed. “Another,” she said.

qa.q: What happened to Harsha's biscuit?
qa.a: It broke and fell on the floor as crumbs.

qa.q: What does Harsha's wobbling lip show she was feeling?
qa.a: It shows sadness or hurt about the biscuit. She might also have been overwhelmed by something else, such as tiredness.

qa.q: What could Uday do if she still cries afterwards?
qa.a: He can stay close, keep his voice gentle and wait until she is ready before offering the new biscuit.

qa.q: What might Harsha feel when Uday opens his arms?
qa.a: She may feel understood and safe, and this may be why her lip stopped shaking.

grounding: A toddler's lower lip trembles before crying from sadness over a broken biscuit, and closeness and a soothing voice help.

subtype: Dropped jaw and open mouth [Expressing]
passage: Layla, eighteen months, stood at the edge of the plaza in Buenos Aires while a street performer blew huge bubbles. Her jaw dropped, her mouth hung open and she didn't blink. Her mother Sofia crouched beside her and watched the bubbles with her. Later at home, Layla sat by the window with her mouth open again, drool running down her chin. She gnawed her fist and grumbled. Sofia wiped her chin and gave her a cool teething ring.

qa.q: Where did Layla watch the bubbles?
qa.a: At the edge of the plaza in Buenos Aires.

qa.q: What might Layla's open mouth at the bubbles show, and how is it different from the later one?
qa.a: At the plaza it likely shows wonder and full attention. Later, with the drool and gnawing on her fist, it more likely shows the discomfort of teething.

qa.q: How did Sofia support Layla in both moments?
qa.a: She shared the wonder by watching with her, and later she wiped her chin and offered something cool to chew on. 🙂

qa.q: What might Sofia think if a stranger said Layla looked rude?
qa.a: She might explain that Layla is simply staring in wonder or has sore gums, so the open mouth is not meant to be disrespectful.

grounding: A toddler stares with a dropped jaw in wonder and drools while teething, showing attention or discomfort.

subtype: Dropped jaw and open mouth [Expressing]
passage: At the railway station I watched a girl of about two, Pooja, standing beside her father Irfan on the platform. As the train slid in, her mouth fell open and stayed open, eyes huge, one hand holding his trouser. Not a sound. Later she sat on his lap, gnawing a knuckle with drool on her chin, and Irfan wiped it away with a cloth. I couldn't tell if the second face was teething or tiredness, but the first was surely awe.

qa.q: Where did the narrator see Pooja?
qa.a: On the railway station platform, with her father Irfan.

qa.q: What does the narrator think Pooja felt watching the train, and how sure are they?
qa.a: The narrator thinks it was awe, shown by the open mouth, huge eyes and silence, and is less sure about the later face, which could be teething or tiredness.

qa.q: What could Irfan do next time a big train arrives?
qa.a: He could stand beside Pooja, name the train and let her watch as long as she wants. If she seems scared he can pick her up.

qa.q: How might Pooja's staring seem to people on the platform?
qa.a: Some may find it charming, and a few might think she is being rude, though at her age it is only interest.

grounding: A toddler stares open-mouthed in wonder at a train and later drools, seen by an observer who cannot be sure of the second cause.

subtype: Sticking out the tongue in play and taste [Expressing]
passage:
“Ankita, look. Look at me.” Francis stuck out his tongue.
Ankita giggled and stuck hers out, crossing her eyes.
“Now it's a race,” said Francis. “Who can go furthest?”
Ankita shrieked and pushed her tongue out until she almost fell over.
Then he gave her a slice of lime. She licked it, screwed up her face, tongue poking out.
“Sour?” he asked.
“Yuck!” she said, and pushed the slice away.

qa.q: What did Francis give Ankita to lick?
qa.a: A slice of lime.

qa.q: What does Ankita's tongue mean in the lime moment, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It probably shows mild disgust at the sour taste, since she said “Yuck” and pushed the slice away. Earlier, the tongue was just play.

qa.q: How could Francis respond next?
qa.a: He could laugh with her, put the lime away and go on with the tongue game, since a stuck-out tongue here is play, not rudeness.

qa.q: What might Ankita feel when Francis copies her?
qa.a: She may feel happy and clever that a grown-up joins in, which makes the game more fun.

grounding: A toddler sticks out her tongue in imitation play and in mild disgust at a sour taste, and the adult copies it playfully.

subtype: Sticking out the tongue in play and taste [Expressing]
passage: Toddler room note, Tuesday. Nikita, two and a half, loved snack time today. She put out her tongue to lick the yoghurt off the spoon, then kept it out and looked at me with a grin. I put out mine. She laughed, and we did it back and forth. Later she tasted a piece of raw carrot and stuck her tongue out again, but this time with a frown, and pushed it aside. I noted the difference. 🙂 Gautam

qa.q: What was Nikita eating when she first stuck out her tongue?
qa.a: She was licking yoghurt off a spoon at snack time.

qa.q: What did Nikita's tongue mean in each case?
qa.a: With the yoghurt it meant play and fun, since she grinned and laughed. With the carrot, the frown and pushed-aside piece suggest mild dislike, though she might also just have been unsure of the texture.

qa.q: How could Gautam use this in his room?
qa.a: Gautam can keep copying the playful tongue and offer the carrot again another day without pressure.

qa.q: How might Nikita's mother see this?
qa.a: She may be pleased to know it is normal play, and that the tongue is not rude at this age.

grounding: A toddler sticks out her tongue in play and to show mild distaste at a taste, and the teacher copies the play.

subtype: Blank look when overwhelmed [Expressing]
passage: On his first morning at the childminder's in Manchester, Tuan, two, stood in the middle of the room with his coat still on. His face was smooth and empty, and his eyes did not follow the toys or the other children. Not a whimper. Daniel, his father, crouched down and found his hand cold and limp. Daniel sat on the floor with him, asked the childminder to turn down the radio and said nothing for a while. After a long time Tuan leaned against him and let out a shaky breath.

qa.q: What was Tuan doing when Daniel crouched down?
qa.a: He was standing in the middle of the room with his coat still on and an empty face.

qa.q: Why might Tuan's blank face suggest more than calm?
qa.a: The empty stare, limp hand and lack of any play suggest he was overwhelmed by the new place. It might also mean tiredness, but his shaky breath afterwards points to strain.

qa.q: What did Daniel do that helped?
qa.a: He sat down with him, asked for the radio to be turned down and stayed quiet, which reduced stimulation and gave closeness.

qa.q: How might the childminder see Tuan's stillness?
qa.a: The childminder might think he is calm and good, and may need Daniel to explain that it is a sign of being overwhelmed.

grounding: A toddler goes blank and still in a new place, a shutdown rather than calm, and closeness and less stimulation help.

subtype: Blank look when overwhelmed [Expressing]
passage: At the wedding hall I noticed Jahnavi, about two, on her father Akash's lap. Half an hour before she had been chattering and pulling at balloons. Now her face was still, eyes half-open, looking at nothing, and she didn't answer when her aunt called her. The band was loud and there were lights everywhere. Akash noticed too. He walked her to the quiet corridor, and I saw her cheek drop against his shoulder. I can't say what she felt, but she didn't look calm to me, just switched off.

qa.q: Where did the narrator see Jahnavi?
qa.a: At the wedding hall, on her father Akash's lap.

qa.q: What does the narrator think Jahnavi's stillness meant, and how sure are they?
qa.a: The narrator thinks Jahnavi was overwhelmed and switched off, not calm, because she had been chatty before and did not answer her aunt. The narrator admits they cannot know for certain.

qa.q: What could Akash do if the party carries on?
qa.a: He could keep quiet breaks for Jahnavi, keep her near him and leave early if she stays withdrawn.

qa.q: How might her aunt feel when Jahnavi does not answer?
qa.a: She may feel puzzled or a bit hurt, until she learns it was the noise and tiredness and not rejection.

grounding: A toddler goes blank and still in a loud, crowded place, and the father reduces stimulation.

subtype: Relaxed face in sleep and comfort [Expressing]
passage: In the shade of a hotel balcony in Dubai, Layla, two, lay against her mother Sofia's chest with her bottle. The bottle slipped down her chin as her eyelids sank. Her forehead smoothed, her mouth fell slightly open, and her small fingers loosened on the cloth. Sofia felt her body get heavier. “There you are,” she whispered, and kept still. Layla's breaths came slow and even, one hand resting on Sofia's arm, and the busy street below seemed far away.

qa.q: Where was Layla lying while she drifted off?
qa.a: Against her mother Sofia's chest on a hotel balcony in Dubai.

qa.q: What does Layla's smooth forehead and loose hand suggest she feels?
qa.a: They suggest she feels comfortable and safe with Sofia. It could also just be plain tiredness, though both can be true.

qa.q: What could Sofia do once Layla is asleep?
qa.a: She could keep still for a while and then lay her down gently, keeping her close. 🙂

qa.q: What might it be like for Sofia holding a sleeping child?
qa.a: She may feel warm and calm, but also aware that she cannot move without waking Layla.

grounding: A toddler's relaxed face while drifting to sleep shows comfort and safety.

subtype: Relaxed face in sleep and comfort [Expressing]
passage: Berth thirteen on the overnight train. Across from me, a woman called Shalini held her small son Lalremsiami, who had been fidgety all evening. Somewhere after the tea seller passed, he stopped moving. His lips parted, his brow smoothed, his cheek pressed into her arm. She kept still so she wouldn't wake him. I don't know what he felt, but he looked completely safe. Later he stirred and blinked at her when she said his name, so I could see he was just sleeping.

qa.q: Where did the narrator see Shalini and her son?
qa.a: On an overnight train, in the berth across from the narrator.

qa.q: What does the narrator think the relaxed face means, and what proves it was ordinary sleep?
qa.a: The narrator thinks he looked safe and comfortable, as his brow smoothed and his lips parted. When he blinked at Shalini after she said his name, it showed he was simply asleep and responsive.

qa.q: Why does the narrator's last remark matter for a caregiver?
qa.a: It shows a still face while asleep is normal, but a still, unresponsive face while he is awake would deserve attention and a doctor's advice if it continues.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel holding him?
qa.a: She may feel tender and protective, and also tired herself after the long evening.

grounding: A toddler's relaxed face in sleep shows comfort and safety, observed by a fellow passenger who confirms he responds when awake.
